findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend the rollback contract (and the later execution slice's acceptance criteria) to assert on post-rollback INTERPRETATION state — after restoring the backup ref, enforce_since re-anchoring is reverted, verify-authorship is re-run, and stale-clone S3 reset is not spuriously re-triggered — not merely that the ref update reverted.
evidence: Rollback is stated as 'the swap is one revertible ref update' and 'immutable backup ref refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date> before the swap' — asserts the ref returns, not the post-rollback enforce_since / signature-interpretation state.

The transformation is a one-way in-place history rewrite that 're-anchor[s] identity.enforce_since to the baseline' and produces a 're-signed baseline checkpoint' — changing how persisted authorship is interpreted (post-rollback-state applicability (b)/(d)).
S3 forces stale clones (>N days) to reset to remote; after a rollback the rewritten-then-reverted remote could re-trigger this reset, compounding loss.
The HARD STOP defers execution to a later approved slice, so the fix is to carry a post-rollback interpretation-state assertion into that slice's acceptance criteria.
findings.finding: The rollback contract asserts the swap is 'one revertible ref update' and stages on a verified shadow branch, but does not assert on the post-rollback INTERPRETATION state: because the rewrite re-signs the baseline and re-anchors identity.enforce_since, restoring the backup ref may leave already-fast-forwarded clones with a mismatched enforce_since / re-triggered stale-clone force-reset (S3/C3), rather than a clean return to pre-reclaim interpretation.
findings.location: Risk / rollback; S2/S3; Acceptance criteria (S3 stale-clone override)
scenarios: A clone fast-forwards to the rewritten (re-anchored enforce_since) history; the operator then rolls back to refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date>; the clone now sees the restored old history as divergent/stale and force-resets a second time, or its local enforce_since no longer matches the restored ledger.
verify-authorship passes on the shadow branch pre-swap, but nobody re-verifies authorship interpretation AFTER a rollback.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In §S2, name the history-rewrite primitive the coalescing builds on (e.g. git filter-repo / git replace-graft / commit-graph) and justify a hand-rolled alternative against it (anti-repackaging), noting scale (235K commits, 408K trees) and merge/mergetag handling.
evidence: Plan S2: 'history coalescing to a re-signed baseline checkpoint = compacted as-of-horizon state + carried authorship_ledger … Broadened from `.retired`-only to commit/tree reclamation (the object-count lever).'
Risk section describes the mechanics ('changes every commit SHA', 'non-FF force-update') but names no tool.

Retrieved: github.com/newren/git-filter-repo — 'git filter-repo is now recommended by the git [project]' as the canonical history-rewrite / repo-shrink tool; also filter-repo-rs, and Git shallow/graft docs (git-scm.com/docs/shallow.html).
search_files 'filter-repo' across repo: (no matches) — no existing internal tooling this reuses.
findings.finding: The S2 'history coalescing to a re-signed baseline checkpoint' mechanism — the plan's actual object-count lever and a git history rewrite — does not name or evaluate the established external tooling purpose-built for reachable-object reduction (git filter-repo, git replace/grafts, commit-graph), so it is unclear whether S2 builds on a proven tool or hand-rolls the rewrite.
findings.location: Mechanism §S2 / 'History coalescing to a re-signed baseline checkpoint'
scenarios: S2 shadow-clone prototype reinvents commit/tree rewriting that git filter-repo already does at scale on a 235K-commit branch.
A reviewer/approver cannot judge whether the coalescing is a battle-tested rewrite or a bespoke one with untested edge cases (merge commits, mergetags, grafts).
findings.suggested_fix: Add a one-line prior-art note to S2: state that coalescing is implemented via `git filter-repo` (git-project-recommended, scales to this object count) with `--commit-callback`/graft-based collapse, or explicitly justify a bespoke rewrite if filter-repo cannot carry the authorship_ledger / re-signing requirement.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the re-signing capability in the DESIGN+PROOF: name the seam/tool that re-signs the coalesced baseline (e.g. `finalize_event` / `git commit-tree -S`), state which signing principal performs it, and clarify when C4 falls back to enforce_since re-anchoring vs carrying the original signature.
evidence: Plan C4: 'its signature is carried in the SNAPSHOT `authorship_ledger` OR `identity.enforce_since` is re-anchored to grandfather it'; S2: 're-signed baseline checkpoint'.

Repo has a signing seam (CHANGELOG.md:605 'Centralize event signing in a shared finalize_event seam with enforce_since') and enforce_since grandfathering (tests/unit/test_identity_enforce_since_grandfather.py), but the plan does not cite finalize_event/verify_authorship as the re-signing route.

Retrieved prior art on the capability: superuser.com/397149 and stackoverflow.com/41882919 — re-signing rewritten commits is done via `git commit-tree -S` / `filter-branch --commit-filter`, and rebase/rewrite is a known cause of lost verified signatures (codegenes.net verified-signatures-gone-after-rebase).
findings.finding: The 're-signed baseline checkpoint' capability is asserted without resolving HOW rewritten commits get valid signatures — re-signing history-rewritten commits requires an available signer/seam, and the plan neither names the signing seam it reuses nor confirms the current environment can back-sign carried authorship.
findings.location: Design/proof C4 + §S2 / 're-signed baseline'; Acceptance 'S2 … re-signed baseline'
scenarios: S2 prototype produces a baseline whose commit-level signatures cannot be regenerated because the rewriting environment lacks the original signing keys, forcing reliance solely on enforce_since re-anchoring — a materially different (and less-verified) trust posture than 'carried signature'.
verify-authorship on the shadow branch passes only because grandfathering hides unsigned commits, masking a signing-capability gap.
